fixes.explanation: Yes, baker, a robe of many colors. Israel loved Joseph more than his other sons, and the text says Joseph was born to him in his old age. A rainbow lover like me hears "many colors" and leans right in. I'd wear that robe around the bakery and let the ovens get jealous. (Genesis 37:3)
No wind in this dream, baker. Joseph says, “…your sheaves gathered around and bowed down to mine.” Nothing blows anywhere in what he tells his brothers. Bowing is the whole picture. (Genesis 37:7)

That's right, friend. Instead of warming up, his brothers were jealous of him. His father, on the other hand, kept in mind what Joseph had said. Jealousy on one side and a father turning it over on the other. (Genesis 37:11)

Yes, baker. First Reuben says, “Let us not take his life.” Then he suggests the pit, and the text says he said it “…so that he could rescue Joseph from their hands and return him to his father.” Reuben is Jacob's firstborn, so he's the oldest of the brothers. (Genesis 37:21-22; 35:23)

Nice guess, friend, but Damascus isn't on this caravan's map. The text says the camels carrying spices, balm and myrrh are on their way down to Egypt. That load of spices is headed to Egypt, plain and simple. (Genesis 37:25)

Nineveh is a fun guess, baker, but the text doesn't send this caravan there. It says the camels, loaded with spices, balm and myrrh, are coming from Gilead on their way down to Egypt. Egypt is the answer the verse gives. (Genesis 37:25)

Yes, sell, baker. Judah, another of Jacob's sons, says, “Come, let us sell him to the Ishmaelites and not lay a hand on him; for he is our brother, our own flesh.” And the brothers agreed. Judah's idea is to sell Joseph instead of killing him, and they go with it. (Genesis 37:26-27)

Right, baker, twenty shekels of silver. That's the price when the brothers pull Joseph out of the pit and sell him to the Ishmaelites. The Ishmaelites then take him to Egypt. Hold onto that number. (Genesis 37:28)

That's not what the text says, baker. Reuben tears his clothes, returns to his brothers and says, “The boy is gone! What am I going to do?” His words go to his brothers there at the pit. (Genesis 37:29-30)

Yes, baker. The brothers slaughtered a young goat and “…dipped the robe in its blood.” Then they sent the robe to their father and said, “We found this…” That's a hard moment, and it's just what the text says. (Genesis 37:31-32)
True, baker. Jacob recognizes the robe and says, “It is my son’s robe!” Then he says, “A vicious animal has devoured him.” It's a painful verse to read. (Genesis 37:33)
It's actually true, friend. Jacob recognized the robe and said, “It is my son’s robe!” He goes on to say, “A vicious animal has devoured him.” Those are his words in the verse. (Genesis 37:33)

That's right, friend. His sons and daughters tried to comfort him, but “…he refused to be comforted.” He says, “No… I will go down to Sheol mourning for my son.” Then the verse closes with “So his father wept for him.” It's a heavy moment. (Genesis 37:35)

Yes, baker, the guard. The Midianites sold Joseph in Egypt to Potiphar, an officer of Pharaoh and captain of the guard. Joseph started the chapter tending flocks with his brothers, and now he's been sold in Egypt. That's a lot of road for one chapter. (Genesis 37:2, 36)
